title: Fire on Carmel (1 Kings 18:20–39)
hook: how long will you limp between two opinions? water-soaked wood, and fire falls

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zarephath: meal and oil that did not run out, until the rain. Your line was the jar did not fail. What did you share from short supply? Day seven hundred thirty-two.

"How long halt ye between two opinions?" Halt is an older English word for limp. How long will you limp along, one foot on each side? Elijah says it on Mount Carmel, to a crowd of his own people, gathered by the king. The drought has gone on and on. On one side stand the prophets of Baal, the god the king and queen have favored. On the other side stands Elijah, alone. He finishes the question: "if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him." And then the line that hangs in the air: "the people answered him not a word." Today, fire on Carmel.

Since words won't move them, Elijah proposes a test. Two altars, two bulls, wood, and no fire. Each side calls on its god, and, in the King James words, "the God that answereth by fire, let him be God." The people finally speak: "It is well spoken." The prophets of Baal go first, and they call from morning until noon, and on into the afternoon. The text's report is short: "there was no voice, nor any that answered." Then Elijah's turn. First he repairs the altar of the LORD that had been broken down, with twelve stones, one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob, in a kingdom now split in two. Then he does something no one would do if they wanted a fire to start. He has water poured over the offering and the wood, and again, and a third time, until it runs down and fills the trench. Then he prays, and it's a short prayer: "Hear me, O LORD, hear me, that this people may know that thou art the LORD God, and that thou hast turned their heart back again." In the line before, he asks that Israel know he is God's servant, yes, but the prayer ends on the people: their hearts, turned back. And the fire falls. In the King James words, it "consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench." The people fall on their faces and say, "The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God." The silence has become an answer. The chapter goes on past this point to a grim ending at the brook Kishon, and readers have wrestled with it. But the question at its center is the one Elijah asked first, about limping: a life lived with one foot on each side, never quite choosing.

Here's the practice: find where you're limping. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one decision you've been circling for a while: a conversation to have or not, a commitment to keep or end, a habit to start or drop. Notice the limp, the one foot on each side, and what it costs you to stay there. You don't have to settle the big question in two minutes. Just name the very next step that would end the waiting. If you pray, you can bring the decision before God. The bell holds the time.
Carmel. The mountain where Elijah asked a silent crowd how long they'd limp between two opinions, soaked his altar, prayed, and watched the fire fall.
Your line: how long, two opinions? Today, take the next step on the decision you named, before the day ends. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Elijah on Mount Carmel in sermons on wholehearted faith, and his question about halting between two opinions is sometimes quoted when preachers speak about indecision.

original.note: Hebrew: how long, the first words of Elijah's question on Carmel (1 Kings 18:21).

trapdoor: what you thought: a fireworks contest on a mountain.
what it means: a people limping between two loyalties, silent when asked to choose, until the fire falls.
what a scholar hears: Elijah rebuilds the broken altar with twelve stones, one per tribe of Jacob's sons (18:30–31), in a kingdom now torn in two.

notes: 'Halt is the old English word for limp' glosses the KJV word; it is not an etymology of the Hebrew. Confirm.
'The god the king and queen have favored' summarizes 1 Kings 16:31–33 and 18:19; confirm.
'From morning until noon, and on into the afternoon' paraphrases 18:26 and 18:29 (until the time of the evening sacrifice).
The slaughter of the prophets of Baal at the brook Kishon (18:40) is outside the outline's range; it is acknowledged in one sentence rather than retold. A Keeper may prefer to cut or expand it.
The story is told as the text tells it (a contest in Israel's own history); the script does not comment on Baal worship or rank any present-day tradition. Teasing in 18:27 is left out.

Editor pass: review matched to the edited day 731; 'old English' corrected to 'older English' (hook and match); 'just split' removed (the split is not recent in the text); 'its God' lowercased for the two sides; varied the repeated 'Notice what...' teach move.

Audit (fresh auditor, serious): 'He doesn't ask to be proved right' contradicted 18:36 ('let it be known ... that I am thy servant, and that I have done all these things at thy word'); rewritten to acknowledge 18:36 while keeping the 18:37 focus on the people's hearts.
